name: Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS)
description: A heritable connective tissue disorder characterised by joint hypermobility, musculoskeletal pain, and soft tissue fragility. The most common EDS subtype. Frequently co-occurs with POTS and MCAS as a triad.
demographics: Predominantly affects women; estimated prevalence 1 in 500 to 1 in 5000; often undiagnosed for years
specialist_type: Connective tissue / genetics specialist or rheumatologist experienced in EDS

name: Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS)
description: A form of dysautonomia characterised by an abnormal increase in heart rate (≥30 bpm) upon standing, without a significant drop in blood pressure. Causes debilitating fatigue, dizziness, palpitations, and exercise intolerance.
demographics: Predominantly affects women aged 15–50; estimated 1–3 million in the US; often triggered by viral illness or physical trauma
specialist_type: Autonomic neurologist or cardiologist specialising in dysautonomia

name: Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS)
description: A condition where mast cells release chemical mediators inappropriately, causing multi-system symptoms including urticaria, GI issues, brain fog, and anaphylaxis. Distinct from systemic mastocytosis.
demographics: Underdiagnosed; affects all ages and genders; often co-occurs with hEDS and POTS (the triad)
specialist_type: Allergist/immunologist experienced in mast cell disorders

name: Myalgic Encephalomyelitis / Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS)
description: A severe multi-system chronic illness characterised by unexplained fatigue not relieved by rest, post-exertional malaise (PEM), cognitive impairment, and orthostatic intolerance. Often triggered by viral infection.
trigger_patterns: post-exertional malaise (PEM) — symptoms worsen 12-48h after exertion
demographics: Affects all demographics; ~2.5 million in the US; women more commonly affected; onset often after viral illness
specialist_type: ME/CFS specialist; internist with chronic illness expertise

name: Fibromyalgia
description: A chronic pain condition characterised by widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and cognitive symptoms (fibro fog). Central sensitisation is a key mechanism.
demographics: Affects 2–4% of the population; predominantly women; often diagnosed alongside other chronic conditions

name: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
description: A chronic autoimmune disease affecting multiple organ systems including skin, joints, kidneys, and nervous system. Characterised by periods of flares and remission.
demographics: 90% female; predominantly onset ages 15–45; higher prevalence in African American, Hispanic, and Asian women

name: Sjögren's Syndrome
description: A systemic autoimmune disease that primarily affects exocrine glands causing dry eyes and dry mouth, but can involve joints, skin, kidneys, and nervous system.
demographics: 90% female; peak onset ages 40–60; affects about 0.5–1% of population

name: Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD)
description: An overlap syndrome with features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis. Characterised by high titres of anti-U1 RNP antibodies.
demographics: Predominantly women; mean onset age 37; relative rarity

name: Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS)
description: An autoimmune hypercoagulable condition characterised by thrombosis and pregnancy morbidity associated with antiphospholipid antibodies. Can occur alone or with SLE.
demographics: Women of childbearing age most affected; associated with recurrent miscarriage and thrombosis

name: Small Fiber Neuropathy (SFN)
description: A condition affecting small nerve fibres causing burning pain, tingling, temperature sensitivity, and autonomic dysfunction. Often idiopathic or autoimmune in young women.
key_biomarkers: skin punch biopsy (reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density)
demographics: All ages; significant overlap with POTS and hEDS populations; often missed

name: Autoimmune Autonomic Ganglionopathy (AAG)
description: An autoimmune attack on autonomic ganglia causing severe autonomic failure including orthostatic hypotension, anhidrosis, GI dysmotility, and bladder dysfunction.
demographics: Rare; affects adults; may be subacute onset following viral illness

name: Hereditary Alpha Tryptasemia (HαT)
description: A recently described genetic trait caused by increased TPSAB1 gene copies, leading to elevated basal serum tryptase. Presents with mast cell activation symptoms, connective tissue features, and dysautonomia.
trigger_patterns: same as MCAS: food, fragrance, heat, stress
demographics: Affects ~5% of the general population; often in the hEDS/POTS/MCAS triad
specialist_type: Allergist/immunologist or geneticist specialising in mast cell disorders

name: Undifferentiated Connective Tissue Disease (UCTD)
description: An early or incomplete form of connective tissue disease with features of SLE, Sjögren's, or other CTDs but not meeting full criteria for any specific diagnosis. Often evolves into a defined CTD.
key_biomarkers: does not meet ACR criteria for SLE etc.
demographics: Predominantly women; onset in young adulthood; 30-40% eventually evolve to defined CTD

name: Raynaud's Phenomenon (Primary and Secondary)
description: Episodic vasospasm of small vessels in response to cold or stress, causing colour changes in fingers and toes (white → blue → red). Primary is benign; secondary is associated with connective tissue disease.
demographics: Very common; 5–10% of women; primary has onset in teens/20s; secondary onset later

name: Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma)
description: An autoimmune disease causing fibrosis of skin and internal organs, Raynaud's phenomenon, and vascular dysfunction. Includes limited (lcSSc) and diffuse (dcSSc) cutaneous subtypes.
demographics: Women predominantly; onset age 30–60; relatively rare

name: Marfan Syndrome
description: A heritable connective tissue disorder caused by FBN1 mutations affecting fibrillin-1, causing tall stature, arachnodactyly, aortic dilation, lens dislocation, and joint laxity.
demographics: Autosomal dominant; 1 in 5000; affects all genders equally; 25% de novo
specialist_type: Connective tissue geneticist or cardiologist with Marfan expertise

name: Loeys-Dietz Syndrome
description: A connective tissue disorder caused by TGFBR1/2 mutations, clinically overlapping with Marfan syndrome but with distinctive features including bifid uvula and arterial tortuosity.
demographics: Autosomal dominant; rarer than Marfan; severe vascular risk even in childhood

name: Vascular Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (vEDS)
description: The most severe EDS subtype, caused by COL3A1 mutations. Characterised by thin translucent skin, easy bruising, and risk of arterial or organ rupture. Distinct from hEDS.
demographics: Autosomal dominant; prevalence 1 in 50,000–200,000; equal gender distribution
specialist_type: Connective tissue geneticist with vascular surgery access

name: Classical Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (cEDS)
description: An EDS subtype caused by COL5A1/COL5A2 mutations with skin hyperextensibility, atrophic scarring, and joint hypermobility. Genetically confirmed unlike hEDS.
demographics: Autosomal dominant; rarer than hEDS; prevalence ~1 in 20,000

name: Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID)
description: The most common symptomatic primary antibody deficiency, characterised by low immunoglobulins and recurrent bacterial infections. Can cause autoimmune features.
demographics: Equal gender distribution; onset typically age 20–40; delayed diagnosis 5–10 years average

name: Dysautonomia (General/Idiopathic)
description: Dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system not meeting criteria for a specific subtype. Includes symptoms of orthostatic intolerance, heart rate variability, GI dysmotility, and temperature dysregulation.
demographics: Affects all demographics; often overlaps with hEDS and MCAS; underdiagnosed

name: Vasovagal Syncope
description: The most common cause of fainting, triggered by emotional stress, pain, or prolonged standing. Caused by an abnormal autonomic reflex causing sudden drop in heart rate and blood pressure.
key_biomarkers: tilt table test (mixed or vasodepressor pattern)
demographics: Very common; affects all ages; often first presentation in adolescence

name: Inappropriate Sinus Tachycardia (IST)
description: A condition where the sinus node fires too rapidly without a physiological cause, causing persistent or episodic high heart rate even at rest, fatigue, and palpitations. Overlaps clinically with POTS.
key_biomarkers: tilt table (differs from POTS: HR elevation not orthostatic)
demographics: Predominantly women; 20–40 age range

name: Hereditary Angioedema (HAE)
description: A rare genetic disorder causing episodic swelling of the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs due to C1 inhibitor deficiency or dysfunction.
demographics: Autosomal dominant; 1 in 10,000–50,000; equal gender; often misdiagnosed as allergy

name: Eosinophilic Oesophagitis (EoE)
description: A chronic immune/antigen-mediated oesophageal disease characterised by eosinophilic infiltration of the oesophageal epithelium, causing food impaction, dysphagia, and reflux.
trigger_patterns: specific food antigens (milk, wheat, egg, soy, nuts, seafood)
demographics: Predominantly men (3:1); children and young adults; often atopic

name: Coeliac Disease
description: An autoimmune enteropathy triggered by dietary gluten (in wheat, barley, rye) causing villous atrophy, malabsorption, and multi-system symptoms.
demographics: 1% prevalence; affects all ages; female predominance in adults; HLA-DQ2/DQ8 association

name: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
description: A chronic pain condition typically affecting a limb, characterised by burning pain, swelling, skin colour/temperature changes, and movement abnormalities. Often follows injury or surgery.
demographics: More common in women; any age; onset typically follows injury

name: Functional Neurological Disorder (FND)
description: Neurological symptoms (weakness, tremor, sensory loss, non-epileptic seizures) with no structural neurological lesion. Now understood as a disorder of brain function rather than a psychiatric condition.
key_biomarkers: positive clinical signs (Hoover sign, tremor entrainment)
demographics: Predominantly young women (2:1); second most common reason to see a neurologist
specialist_type: Neurologist with FND expertise; multi-disciplinary rehabilitation

name: Multiple Sclerosis (MS)
description: A chronic autoimmune demyelinating disease of the CNS causing relapsing-remitting or progressive neurological disability. Presents with fatigue, sensory symptoms, optic neuritis, and motor weakness.
key_biomarkers: MRI brain and spine (lesions disseminated in space and time)
demographics: Women 3:1 over men; onset typically 20–40; higher prevalence in northern latitudes

name: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD)
description: A severe autoimmune CNS disease targeting aquaporin-4 water channels in the optic nerves and spinal cord. Distinct from MS with different management requirements.
demographics: Predominantly women (9:1); non-Caucasian populations more affected; onset 30–40 years

name: Hashimoto's Thyroiditis
description: An autoimmune thyroiditis causing hypothyroidism, fatigue, brain fog, weight gain, and cold intolerance. The most common cause of hypothyroidism in developed countries.
demographics: 5–10x more common in women; most common in ages 30–50; strong family history
specialist_type: Endocrinologist or GP with thyroid expertise

name: Addison's Disease (Primary Adrenal Insufficiency)
description: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex causing deficiency of cortisol and aldosterone. Causes profound fatigue, salt craving, orthostatic hypotension, and skin hyperpigmentation.
demographics: Rare (1 in 10,000); slightly more common in women; autoimmune form in adults

name: Dermatomyositis
description: An inflammatory myopathy with distinctive skin rashes (Gottron's papules, heliotrope rash) and proximal muscle weakness. Associated with malignancy in adults.
demographics: Bimodal onset (childhood and 40–60 years); women 2:1; malignancy screen essential in adults

name: Polymyositis
description: An inflammatory myopathy without the distinctive skin changes of dermatomyositis. Causes proximal muscle weakness, fatigue, and elevated muscle enzymes.
demographics: Predominantly adults over 20; women slightly more affected

name: Sarcoidosis
description: A granulomatous disease of unknown cause that can affect virtually any organ, most commonly lungs, lymph nodes, skin, and eyes. Presents with fatigue, cough, skin lesions, and joint pain.
demographics: Young to middle-aged adults; higher prevalence in African Americans; women slightly more affected

name: Behçet's Disease
description: A rare multisystem vasculitis characterised by recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, eye inflammation, and skin lesions. Can cause CNS and vascular involvement.
demographics: Higher prevalence along Silk Road (Turkey, Iran, Japan); onset 20–40 years; more severe in men

name: Stiff Person Syndrome
description: A rare autoimmune neurological disorder causing progressive muscle stiffness and painful spasms, particularly affecting the trunk and limbs. Often associated with anti-GAD65 antibodies.
demographics: Middle-aged adults; women 2:1; rare (1–2 per million)

name: Anti-NMDA Receptor Encephalitis
description: A severe autoimmune encephalitis caused by antibodies against NMDA receptors, presenting with psychiatric symptoms, seizures, movement disorders, and autonomic instability. Often follows viral illness or teratoma.
key_biomarkers: anti-NMDA receptor antibodies in CSF (gold standard)
demographics: Young women predominate; median age 21; ovarian teratoma in ~50% of adult women

name: PANDAS / PANS
description: Paediatric Acute-onset Neuropsychiatric Syndrome (PANS) and its streptococcal-triggered subtype (PANDAS). Characterised by sudden onset OCD, tics, cognitive changes, and emotional dysregulation following infection.
demographics: Children and adolescents; affects both genders
specialist_type: Paediatric neurologist or psychiatrist with PANS/PANDAS expertise

name: Gastroparesis
description: Delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction, causing nausea, vomiting, bloating, and early satiety. Can be idiopathic, diabetic, or autonomic in origin.
key_biomarkers: gastric emptying scintigraphy (>10% retention at 4 hours)
demographics: More common in women; associated with prior viral illness; strong overlap with dysautonomia

name: Crohn's Disease
description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the GI tract with transmural inflammation, causing abdominal pain, diarrhoea, fatigue, and malabsorption.
demographics: Onset typically 15–35 years; equal gender distribution; higher in northern latitudes and Western populations

name: Ulcerative Colitis
description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease affecting the colon and rectum with mucosal inflammation, causing bloody diarrhoea, urgency, cramping, and fatigue.
demographics: Onset 15–35 years; equal gender distribution; higher in northern latitudes

name: Hyperadrenergic POTS
description: A subtype of POTS characterised by excessive sympathetic nervous system activation on standing, causing disproportionate rise in blood pressure along with heart rate. Presents with tremor, anxiety-like symptoms, and palpitations.
key_biomarkers: BP may increase on standing (vs. normal drop)
demographics: Subset of POTS patients; may have NET (norepinephrine transporter) mutation

name: Neuropathic POTS (Autoimmune)
description: A POTS subtype caused by partial denervation of lower extremity vasculature, leading to venous pooling. Often triggered by viral illness; may have autoimmune small-fibre neuropathy.
demographics: Young women; strong post-COVID-19 association; post-infectious onset

name: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD)
description: A rare systemic inflammatory disease characterised by quotidian fever, evanescent salmon-coloured rash, and joint involvement. Part of the autoinflammatory spectrum.
demographics: Young adults (2 peaks: 15–25 and 36–46 years); equal gender

name: Relapsing Polychondritis
description: A rare autoimmune disorder causing recurrent inflammation of cartilaginous structures including ears, nose, joints, and the tracheobronchial tree.
demographics: Middle age; equal gender; often misdiagnosed

name: Lupus Nephritis
description: Kidney inflammation occurring as a complication of SLE. Presents with proteinuria, haematuria, and renal impairment. Requires specific monitoring and treatment.
demographics: Occurs in ~50% of SLE patients; more severe in certain ethnicities and men with SLE

name: Autoimmune Hepatitis
description: A chronic inflammatory liver disease of unknown cause where the immune system attacks hepatocytes, leading to cirrhosis if untreated.
demographics: Bimodal onset (adolescence and middle age); women 70–80%

name: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)
description: A chronic cholestatic liver disease caused by autoimmune destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to liver cirrhosis if untreated.
demographics: 90–95% women; onset typically 40–60 years; strong family history

name: Graves' Disease
description: The most common cause of hyperthyroidism, caused by TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies. Presents with weight loss, palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance, and ophthalmopathy.
key_biomarkers: TSH suppressed / T4 and T3 elevated
demographics: Women 7–10:1 over men; onset typically 20–50 years

name: Hypovolemic POTS
description: A POTS subtype characterised by reduced blood volume as the primary driver of orthostatic tachycardia. May respond particularly well to fluid/salt loading.
trigger_patterns: menstrual cycle (oestrogen effect on blood volume)
demographics: Young women; often associated with low body weight

name: Seronegative Spondyloarthropathy
description: A group of related inflammatory arthritides including ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and reactive arthritis, characterised by spinal inflammation, enthesitis, and skin/gut involvement.
demographics: Young adults; stronger male predominance in classic AS; women equally affected in axial spondyloarthropathy

name: Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1 (DM1)
description: The most common adult muscular dystrophy, caused by CTG repeat expansion in the DMPK gene. Causes myotonia, progressive muscle weakness, cardiac arrhythmias, cataracts, and GI dysmotility.
demographics: Most common adult muscular dystrophy; autosomal dominant; variable penetrance; anticipation
